The seventh meeting of the Disarmament and International Security Committee, the first committee of the 80th session of the General Assembly, is called to order. Distinguished delegates, the committee will continue this afternoon with its general debate on all disarmament and international security agenda items allocated to it. Allow me to remind delegations that the deadline for submission of all draft resolutions and decisions was today at noon. We will now turn to our list of speakers for today and I urge all delegations taking the floor to kindly keep in mind the suggested time limit for statements. I now give the floor to His Excellency the Permanent Representative to the Conference on Disarmament of Italy. Excellency, you have the floor.

Thank you, Vice-Chair. Italy aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union. I will now add some remarks in my national capacity. We gather this year as the United Nations marks its 80th anniversary amid a gravely deteriorated security context. It is a trend that we have witnessed over the last few years and that requires renewed commitment on our part to reverse. The multilateral disarmament machinery that we have built over decades must now be preserved and protected against all threats. Chief among those threats, Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, but also its unacceptable nuclear saber-rattling that we continue to condemn in the strongest terms. Earlier this year, as in 2024, Moscow vetoed the participation of 15 EU member states and candidate countries as observers to the Conference on Disarmament. This was an unprecedented affront to the multilateral system and the principle of inclusivity. Vice Chair, we commend President Trump's negotiating efforts and the mediation of Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey, which led to the signing on Monday in Sharm El-Sheikh of the first phase of the peace plan. The cessation of hostilities, the release of the hostages and the resumption of humanitarian aid are crucial steps as we now look to the longer term. Italy stands ready to participate in an international stabilization mission and to contribute to Gaza's reconstruction, sparing no effort to achieve the two state solution as the only path to lasting peace. Vice Chair. Italy shares the goal of a peaceful and secure world completely free of nuclear weapons. Article 6 of the NPT provides the necessary legal framework. There is no alternative instrument to the NPT. In under seven months, we will gather here for its eleventh review conference. The previous conference and the meetings of the Preparatory Committee have clearly shown how difficult it is to find agreement on a broad range of issues. In fact, consensus has been elusive for the past 15 years. Italy believes that we should now find the right balance between ambition and realism. The Review Conference should provide an opportunity for all States Parties to recommit to the core goals and principles of the NPT. As a staunch supporter of the CTBT, Italy urges all states that have not yet done so to sign and ratify the treaty without further delay and in the meantime to respect the moratorium on nuclear tests. It is also time we started long overdue negotiations on an FMCT in the CD. Italy believes that Iran should never possess nuclear weapons and urges Tehran to return to full and unhindered cooperation with the IAEA and to the negotiating table. All enriched fissile material must be accounted for. It is imperative to find a diplomatic way forward. We are also seriously concerned at the irresponsible behaviour of the DPRK, which represents a serious threat to international peace and security. We urge Pyongyang to take concrete steps towards a complete, verifiable and irreversible denuclearisation. Vice-Chair, almost three years ago, the main result of the ninth review conference of the Biological Weapons Convention was the establishment of a working group to strengthen it. We now have a concrete and attainable goal before us to adopt the two mechanisms respectively on international cooperation and assistance and on science and technology. This should be done at a special conference to be convened hopefully in August 2026 as proposed by the chair of the working group. That special conference should also chart the way forward on compliance and verification by establishing a separate working group to address exclusively this crucial aspect. The military use of new and emerging technologies is becoming a priority issue. We support the ongoing work of the GGE on laws and are heartened to see that the two-tier approach is gaining traction. The eventual goal of this process should be the adoption of a protocol to the CCW. We also believe that the time has come to discuss the broader issue of military applications of new technologies, in particular AI, and to identify the right forum to do this. Italy remains strongly committed to supporting the CWC and the work of the OPCW. We strongly condemn any use of chemical weapons anywhere, at any time, by anyone, under any circumstances. Outer space security remains a top priority for us. The open-ended working group has started substantive work last July. We view the behavioral and the capabilities approaches as complementary in addressing the same threats. As far as the normative framework is concerned, Italy believes that urgent and serious consideration should be given to the idea of a legally binding instrument banning direct ascent anti-satellite tests in outer space. Chair, Vice-Chair, during Italy's presidency of the Conference on Disarmament earlier this year, five subsidiary bodies were established to deal with a main topic on the CD's agenda. It was the first time since 1996 that such a decision was taken in January and the sixth time that it was taken at all during the same period. While we regret that the subsidiary bodies were unable to agree on a report, our assessment of this year's session is not entirely negative. Delegations actively engaged in intensive debates and that work could form the basis for renewed discussions next year in a spirit of continuity. Many complain that the CD is in a deadlock. This is true, but it is also true that this is not the CD's fault. This is the result of deep divisions at the international level and of the abuse of the consensus rule. While we wait for the right time and the right conditions to restart our negotiating role, we should not renounce this opportunity to exchange views and seek common ground. This is all we have now, but it is important to safeguard it. Chair, the Ottawa Convention on Anti-Personnel Mines and the Oslo Convention on Cluster Munitions, two core humanitarian disarmament treaties, are facing unprecedented challenges. In its view, Increasing international tension and conflicts make the imperative of a world free of anti-personnel mines and cluster munitions even more urgent, and we renew our support to the principles and objectives enshrined in the Conventions and to their universalisation. Across all these issues, Italy highly values greater interaction with civil society and a gender perspective as a key contribution to our work. I thank you, Vice-Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Italy for his statement. I now give the floor to His Excellency, the Permanent Representative of the Syrian Arab Republic. Excellency, you have the floor.

I congratulate you on your election as chair of the first committee. I also extend my congratulations to the members of your bureau and I wish to assure you of our full support to ensure the success of this session. My delegation aligns itself with the statements delivered by the Arab Group and with the statement made on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. Chairman, the Syrian Arab Republic believes that multilateral action consistent with the Charter is the only sustainable path to addressing disarmament and international security issues. This conviction is particularly important in light of the serious challenges that we face in the world today, particularly in our region and the threats to peace and security caused by the Israeli occupation authorities violating the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Syria. They are interfering in our internal affairs and taking advantage of the transition period in order to make political gains. This is coinciding also with the suffering of our brothers and sisters on the Gaza Strip, and the international community must work together to put an end to this situation. We welcome the ceasefire agreement in Gaza. And we hope that this development will enable us to lift the suffering of civilians and will allow us to continue to deliver humanitarian aid, paving the way towards regional stability. We express our appreciation to Qatar, Turkey, Turkey, Egypt and the United States, who all contributed to reaching this agreement. Chairman, the Syrian Arab Republic reaffirms its steadfast commitment to cooperating with the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the OCPW. It condemns the use of chemical weapons at all times, anywhere, by anyone, under any circumstances. In the new Syria, my colleagues working on this file in Damascus and in the relevant ministries concerning the elimination of the chemical arsenal of the Assad regime, many of whom are survivors and witnesses of the use of these weapons, have become guarantors of truth and justice for the victims. And they are determined to ensure that such a tragedy isn't allowed to happen again and that we can rid Syria and the rest of the world of these abject weapons. This process led to Syria launching a new phase of cooperation following the fall of the Assad regime, demonstrating clear political will to turn the page of the past. Syria has succeeded in transforming its relationship with the international community from one of skepticism to one of partnership in achieving the goals of non-proliferation. This transformation was anchored by the reception of the OPCW Director General by the President of the Republic in February, leading a large delegation from the organization. Since then, Syria has hosted six teams of the Technical Secretariat looking to their deployment. One was cancelled due to the Israeli attack targeting the Ministry of Defense in Damascus. Because the Ministry of Defense is the party, the ministry that is supporting the OPCW on the ground. What's more, the Syrian government And this is an historic first. Through the permanent mission of our brother country, Qatar submitted a draft decision to the OPCW titled Accelerating On-Site Destruction of Any Remaining Chemical Weapons in the Syrian Arab Republic. This project was co-sponsored by 53 other countries and was adopted by consensus during the session of the Executive Council of the OPCW at its 110th session which took place at the beginning of this month. In this spirit, Syria, the Syrian government has also submitted a conceptual plan for the destruction and verification of any remaining chemical weapons and other legacy items from the Assad era. This work was also done with the support of the Qatari mission in this context chairman and given that history is written through international resolutions resolutions that reflect the suffering of peoples it is important for the resolution that will be presented to this committee to refer to the suffering of the Syrian people at the hands of chemical weapons which is why we call on all states to support this decision in order to rid Syria and the whole of the world of chemical weapons so that our people may be able to feel the support of the international community and so that our people aren't ignored and that we don't ignore this aspect of things. The Assad regime shrouded the chemical weapons program in secrecy, drawing on complex security architecture that was designed in order for them to dodge their obligations under the convention. And this made identifying and accessing the sites particularly difficult and risky. And the legacy that was left behind by the Al-Assad regime is one of them not complying. And there are also issues to do with economic recovery. The Assad regime left the country with significant stumbling blocks in eliminating the explosive remnants of war. And we require the international community to be mobilized in order to provide the resources, the equipment, the material and technical support also in order to support the efforts of the Syrian government and the OPCW. Chairman, Syria as a state party to the NPT considers that this treaty is a cornerstone of the global disarmament and non-proliferation regime given the situation in the Middle East region the countries of our region need to cooperate in order to build a better world and a better future for our region and this is why Syria attaches particular importance to international cooperation under international law and the UN Charter. The speaker's microphone was cut off, say the interpreters.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Syrian Arab Republic for his statement. I now give the floor to His Excellency, the Permanent Representative of the Lao People's Democratic Republic. Excellency, you have the floor.

The Chair, at the outset, I would like to congratulate the Chair, Vice-Chairs, and members of the Bureau on your election to lead the first Committee. We are confident in your leadership and reaffirm our delegation's full support and cooperation. My delegation aligns itself with the statements delivered by representatives of Uganda and Malaysia on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement and ASEAN respectively. Mr. Chair, the current international security landscape continues to be complex and volatile, marked by ongoing tensions and conflicts in many parts of the world. We share the concern over the rising global military expenditure which heightens tensions rather than promotes peace and security. It is therefore imperative to reaffirm our commitment to multilateralism upon the UN Charter and fulfill our obligations under multilateral disarmament treaties to prevent future catastrophes. The Lao PDR reiterates its unwavering support for global efforts to achieve a world free of nuclear weapons. We regard the NPT as the cornerstone of nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation, and the peaceful use of nuclear energy. We extend our congratulations to Ambassador Do Hong Viet of Vietnam on his designation as President of the 2026 NPT Review Conference, and look forward to working closely with him and his team. The Lao PDR remains firmly committed to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material and its amendment, and the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapon-Free Zone Treaty. We emphasized the complementarity nature of the TPNW with other key instruments, including the NPT, the CTBT, and nuclear weapon-free zone treaties. We underscored the importance of the full and effective implementation of all instruments related to weapons of mass destruction, including Security Council Resolution 1540. The Lao PDR remains fully committed to the Chemical Weapons Convention and the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention and believes our nations share a collective responsibility to uphold these norms. The Chair, while emerging technologies offer significant benefits, They also present new risks to international peace and security, particularly in cyberspace and outer space. We support the establishment of comprehensive frameworks to ensure these domains are used exclusively for peaceful purposes. The open-ended working group on the security of and in the use of ICTs has played a vital role in promoting international cooperation and capacity building in cybersecurity. We welcome the consensus adoption of its final report and the establishment of a global mechanism on ICT security. The Lao PDR stands ready to contribute to this important process. On small arms and light weapons, we welcome progress made under the global framework for through-life conventional ammunition management. the fourth review conference of the UN Programme of Action and the International Tracing Instrument. Mr. Chair, for over five decades, the Lao PDR has endured the devastating impact of cluster munitions. Unexploded ordnance, or UXO, continues to impact development and endanger life. The Convention on Cluster Munitions has brought renewed hope. Our national strategy, Safe Path Forward III, 2021-2030, aligns with the CCM and the Lawson Action Plan, integrating UXO action into our broader development agenda, including through our national SDG 18, Life Safe from UXO. Partnerships with the state parties, international organizations, and civil society have been instrumental in clearing contaminated land, delivering risk education, supporting survivors and facilitating the return of land for agriculture and infrastructure development. For the Lao PDR, the CCM is more than a disarmament treaty. It is a path to peace, development and dignity. We are honoured to assume the presidency and the host of the third review conference of state parties to the CCM in Vientiane in 2026. This is both a historic responsibility and opportunity to reaffirm our global unity in the fight against cluster munitions. In conclusion, the Lao PDR believes that with strong political will and renewed commitment, we can advance the global disarmament and non-proliferation agenda. We stand ready to engage constructively in the work of the First Committee in pursuit of our shared vision for a peaceful and secure world. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Lao People's Democratic Republic. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Greece. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Vice Chair. Allow me to congratulate you and the Bureau on your election. You can count on Greece's full support in steering the work of the First Committee during this landmark 80th session. We also express our appreciation to Ambassador Maritza Tzanova Valverde of Costa Rica for her skillful leadership of last year's session. Greece aligns fully with the statement delivered by the European Union and wishes to add the following remarks in its national capacity. As the United Nations celebrates its 80th anniversary, the international legal order based on international law and the UN Charter is under severe strain. For nearly four years, Europe has endured its most devastating conflict since World War II. Greece continues to condemn Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and supports all efforts to bring it to a just and lasting end. We welcome the recent US-led peace initiative and urge Russia to engage in good faith negotiations. We also welcome the historic agreement reached between Israel and Hamas on the first phase of the Gaza peace plan, leading to a ceasefire, increased humanitarian assistance, and the release of hostages. Greece remains deeply concerned by ongoing humanitarian crisis and grave human rights violations in Sudan, the Sahel, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Yemen, and elsewhere. Mr. Vice Chair, the international community must uphold and strengthen the global disarmament and non-proliferation architecture, which faces both traditional and emerging challenges. Persistent obstruction by certain states continues to paralyze key mechanisms of the disarmament machinery. As a non-permanent member of the Security Council, Greece is firmly committed to safeguarding and advancing this architecture. We reaffirm our unwavering support for the Treaty of the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, the cornerstone of global disarmament and non-proliferation. The preservation and universalization of the NPT, a balanced approach to its three pillars, and genuine dialogue between nuclear and non-nuclear states should guide our work towards the 11th review conference. We commend the International Atomic Energy Agency for its impartial efforts to ensure compliance with safeguards agreements and the additional protocol, and we support universal adherence to both. A key step toward nuclear disarmament would be the entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. Greece calls on all states that have not yet done so to ratify it and maintain a moratorium on nuclear test explosions. We also urge the early commencement of negotiations on the Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty and dialogue on the successor to New START. Greece continues to support the effective implementation of Security Council Resolution 1540. As Vice-Chair of the 1540 Committee, we focus on preventing the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their delivery means to non-state actors, including terrorists. We remain concerned about Iran's nuclear program and call on Iran to fulfill its legal obligations under the NPT and cooperate fully with the IAEA. As chair of the sanctions committee established under resolution 1718, Greece is committed to upholding the sanctions regime on the DPRK as an essential tool to constrain its WMD and ballistic missile programs. We are ready to work with all partners toward the complete verifiable and irreversible denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. It is imperative to strengthen multilateral instruments prohibiting chemical and biological weapons. Greece supports the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons in carrying out its mandate impartially and professionally and encourages full cooperation to resolve all outstanding issues related to Syria's chemical weapons file. Greece remains a strong supporter of key conventional arms control instruments, including the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention, the Arms Trade Treaty, and the UN Programme of Action on Small Arms and Light Weapons. We also welcome the establishment of the global framework on through-life conventional ammunition management aimed at preventing diversion and unintended explosions. Mr. Vice Chair, the digital transformation has brought immense opportunities for growth, inclusion, and sustainable development, but also unprecedented security risks. Malicious behavior in cyberspace has intensified, including attacks targeting critical infrastructure and becoming part of armed conflict operations. We must respond collectively by implementing the UN framework for responsible state behavior in cyberspace. Greece welcomes the consensus final report of the open-ended working group and the establishment of the global mechanism on developments in the field of ICTs. We remain committed to an open, secure, and peaceful cyberspace governed by international law and look forward to advancing responsible state behavior under the new global mechanism. The peaceful use of emerging technologies, especially artificial intelligence, offers great promise but also serious risk of miscalculation and misuse. Greece advocates for a human-centric AI agenda based on transparency, ethics, and accountability. In April, Greece convened a Security Council ARIA formula meeting on harnessing safe, inclusive, and trustworthy AI for international peace and security. We welcome the Secretary General's report on AI in the military domain and support the forthcoming first committee resolution on this issue. We also stress the urgency of progress on lethal autonomous weapons systems within the CCW framework and the group of governmental experts and reiterate that the peaceful use of outer space must prevail over any militarization. In the spirit of the UNAD initiative, revitalizing the disarmament machinery is more urgent than ever. Greece supports practical proposals to improve the efficiency of the first committee, including rationalising debate time and modernising its structure. We believe the time has come to adjust the current cluster system, reflecting decades old realities, by dedicating a standalone cluster to emerging technologies. Mr. Vice-Chair, Greece remains resolute in its commitment to uphold and strengthen the global disarmament and non-proliferation regime. Only by reinforcing trust in international law and revitalizing multilateralism can we move closer to our shared vision of general and complete disarmament. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Greece for his statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Let me begin by extending my delegation's warm congratulation to you and other members of the Bureau on your election to guide the work of the committee. We are confident that under your able leadership, our deliberations will be both productive and impactful. Please be assured of the full support and cooperation of my delegation throughout the course of the committee work. I also express my delegation's appreciation to Ambassador Marisa Chan Valverde for her able and skillful leadership during the 69th session. My delegation aligns itself with the statement delivered by the Republic of Uganda on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement and the Republic of Guinea-Bissau on behalf of the African Group, respectively. Mr. Chairman, the current global security landscape is mired into complex challenges, which pose serious threat to international peace and security. The fact that the International Committee fails to make concrete progress on disarmament makes our collective task of ensuring international security difficult. Today we witness the threat of nuclear weapons intensified at a breath and continued modernization and stockpiling of weapons of mass destruction, including conventional weapons. We all agree the only way to curb these challenges is by committing to the full implementation of all relevant international treaties and conventions. It should be our collective responsibility to make sure that the disarmament machinery does in fact work by restoring its credibility and effectiveness. Conference on disarmament is and should remain the single multilateral negotiating forum for disarmament. In this regard, we urge for renewed political will and commitment to overcome the deadlock that has long hindered CD substantive work. Ethiopia also believes that continued discussion between nuclear and non-nuclear weapon states must be strengthened to accelerate progress in our collective efforts to realize a nuclear free world. We must therefore strive in our endeavor to achieve successful outcome at the next year NPT review conference. As a state party to the African Nuclear Weapon Free Zone Treaty, Ethiopia reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the treaty and work with all to ensure a region free of nuclear weapons and use nuclear science and technology for peaceful purpose to promote our continent's socioeconomic development. Mr. Chairman, peaceful use of outer space is critical for future of humanity and to ensure sustainable development. Ethiopia therefore underscores the need to excel in our effort to harness outer space for the benefit of humanity and work to prevent arm race in outer space. through the establishment of a legally binding instrument. This should be done by reinforcing existing international legal framework in accordance with the United Nations treaty governing outer space activities. We also call on the United Nations to enhance its effort to ensure that the necessary support, particularly to African countries, is made available to enable them develop their capacity in space science and technology. In the same vein, we should not fall short in our collective efforts of strengthening transparency and confidence building measures and ensure equitable access to the space technologies, particularly by developing countries. We also believe by harnessing emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence within the globally agreed frameworks, we can make effective use of innovation to ensure sustainable peace, equity, and development. In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, EITI PRI affirms its steadfast commitment to fulfilling its international treaty obligations and to contributing constructively to the deliberations of this committee. We remain hopeful that this session will yield concrete progress in advancing global peace and security. for present and future generations. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ethiopia for his statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Haiti. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Vice Chair, on behalf of my delegation. I warmly congratulate you on your election. to the Bureau of this first committee, and we assure you and the Bureau of our full support as we carry on our work. My delegation welcomes the report of the Secretary-General of the United Nations on the various agenda items relating to disarmament and international security. Haiti aligns itself with these statements made by Belize on behalf of CARICOM and Indonesia on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. We would like to add our voice, the voice of a country facing an unprecedented security crisis fueled by the unchecked proliferation of illicit weapons, weak international controls, and the rise of transnational organized crime. The Republic of Haiti reaffirms its commitment to the NPT. We call for its comprehensive implementation. We commend progress made with regard to the TPNW and support multilateral, transparent, irreversible and verifiable disarmament. Similarly, we call for the immediate entry into effect of the CTBT. Mr. Vice Chair, despite significant progress made with regard to the program of action on SALW and its international tracing instrument, the Arms Trade Treaty, the global framework on the management of conventional ammunition, as well as regional relationships such as the Roadmap of the Caribbean for 2030, as well as efforts to combat illicit trafficking in SALW, Our efforts remain confronted by persistent challenges. The security crisis that has been raging in Haiti has been putting the effectiveness of these instruments to the test. Despite their existence, we continue to stand helplessly by as we see an unchecked proliferation of SALW in the region and our country in particular. This constant inflow of illicit weapons runs counter to both the spirit and the letter of the international instruments that we have adopted together. To this end, we call for heightened support for national capacity building, especially when it comes to traceability, collection and destruction of SALW, and the implementation of recommendations from the SG's report. That is paragraph 100V of resolution 79/54 of the General Assembly on the global framework for conventional munitions management throughout their life cycle. Rigorous and universal application of the ATT, strengthen regional cooperation based on information sharing, operational coordination and technical assistance. We commend the efforts made by UNODC, UNLIREC and CARICOM IMPACS, especially their pivotal support to the Haitian security forces. Haiti remains strongly committed to the implementation of its National Action Plan and will continue to work together with its partners to build lasting peace and shared security throughout the region. Haiti is troubled by the risks posed by emerging military technology, especially lethal autonomous weapon systems. AI in the military field and cyber threats. These threats compromise peace, security and international law, especially for the most vulnerable states. Haiti reaffirms its commitment to ethical and human disarmament. We also would like to underscore the importance of equitable participation by countries, developing countries, when it comes to governance of these technologies in accordance with the UN Charter and Resolution 79/1. We also reaffirm our commitment to promoting nuclear weapons free zones, which are a crucial pillar of regional and global stability. Haiti remains fully committed to the Tlatelolco Treaty, which has been in effect since 1975, and we support efforts to establish a similar zone in the Middle East in accordance with resolution 73/546. The Republic of Haiti remains convinced that only that lasting disarmament can only be achieved through a collective, inclusive approach that is based on international solidarity. We support initiatives that promote the participation of young people and gender equality. These human dimensions are crucial for building a truly lasting peace that is centred on human dignity. Mr Vice-Chair, the agenda of this committee ought to serve as a real roadmap for our collective security. Therefore, Haiti calls for focusing on the following points: 99Q, combating illicit trafficking of small arms; 99O, assistance to States in their collection and destruction; and the implementation of the Arms Trade Treaty. These measures are directly linked to the daily reality. lived by the Haitian people. It is time to move from commitments to actions and to translate our resolutions into tangible, coordinated, ambitious action. In closing, the Republic of Haiti reaffirms that disarmament is a necessary prerequisite for a lasting peace, the resilience of fragile states, and respect for human dignity. We remain firmly committed to working with all Member States to transform norms into tangible reality in the spirit of the UN Charter and for the benefit of current and future generations. Let's make disarmament not a faraway goal but a concrete reality. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Haiti for her statement. Merci beaucoup. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Maldives. You have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. I congratulate you and the Bureau on your election. You have full support and cooperation of Maldives in the work of the Committee. The Maldives aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uganda on behalf of NAM. We are witnessing a reversal in disarmament. Key treaties are weakening, arsenals are expanding with new technologies, rising tensions are eroding trust and dialogue. while military budgets reach record levels and divert resources from people's most basic needs. Disarmament is not a choice, it's a responsibility. We must restore trust, new dialogue, and redirect resources from weapons to development. To that end, action is needed on three fronts. First, recommit to nuclear disarmament. Withdrawal of arms control treaties at a time when nuclear weapons grow more powerful, precise and accessible are deeply alarming. Such actions unravel decades of progress and push the world closer to instability. We urge nuclear-armed states to renew dialogue and recommit to disarmament treaties, starting with ratifying the CTBT and adopting no-first-use policies. They must present clear, transparent and time-bound plans to eliminate nuclear stockpiles. Every delay carries a price, one that could cost innocent lives and the very foundation of peace. While nuclear-armed states must lead, all Treaty Parties share responsibility to uphold commitment and ensure accountability. The Maldives fulfills its obligation by ratifying key treaties and enacting national laws. We also call for urgent action to address the environmental dangers of nuclear waste transport and disposal. For island states where healthy oceans are lifelines, this threat is existential. Together, we must ensure the 2026 review conference of the parties to the non-proliferation treaty delivers measurable outcome. Second, Regulate emerging technologies. The arms race has moved beyond land, sea, and air into the cyberspace and outer space. Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons systems, are advancing faster than the framework to govern them. Unchecked, they could transform warfare and erode humanitarian legal and ethical boundaries. Israel's genocide in Gaza shows what is at stake. AI-enabled targeting systems have reportedly been used against civilians, blurring lines between surveillance and warfare, and accelerating decisions with limited human oversight. We must close the governance gap through inclusive, transparent, and binding rules that ensure accountability, prevent misuse, and promote responsible innovations. Technology must serve humanity, saving lives, advancing health, creating opportunities. That is why the Maldives joins the International Atomic Energy Agency, believing in nuclear science for peaceful purpose, including cancer treatment. Third, rebalancing spending from weapons to development. Last year, more than 100 countries increased defense spending. Global military expenditure reaches $2.7 trillion. The Secretary General's report on disarmament warns that if current trend continues, it will rise to $6.6 trillion by 2035. Redirecting even a fraction of this would transform lives. $93 million a year, less than 4% of military expenditure, could end hunger by 2030 in low income countries. $5 trillion could fund 12 years of quality education for every child in these countries. The challenge before us is not a shortage of means, but a shortage of moral clarity. Redirecting resources from military spending towards sustainable development is essential to getting this SDG back on track. For SEEDS, fair and affordable access to finance is the difference between debt and development, between fragility and resilience. When resources, instead of weapons, flows to people, the world becomes safer. The Maldives remains committed to work with partners to strengthen counter proliferation efforts and uphold the rule of law. Our collective security cannot rest on weapons. It must rest on trust, built through dialogue, cooperation and respect for binding commitments. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Maldives for his statement and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Liberia. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. I congratulate you and the other members of the Bureau on your election and assure you of my delegation's full support throughout this session. Liberia aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the African Group. and I make the following remarks in my national capacity. Indeed, the first committee General Assembly remains a vital global platform where we converge annually to discuss and reaffirm our shared commitment to peace, security, and human rights. This year, we convene at a time when the world stands at the edge of a dangerous height with rising geopolitical rivalries, armed conflicts, human rights violations, and blatant disregard for our multilateral system. Liberia underscores the significance of the United Nations disarmament machinery as the driving force of the multilateral disarmament architecture emphasizing renewed commitment to the multilateral system and initiatives guided by our collective pursuit of lasting peace and security. Liberia's stance on nuclear disarmament remains unchanged. It is inspired by that which unite us as a people with a common objective, the preservation of humanity, and the protection of our one world. While the persistent failure of the United Nations Disarmament Commission to reach consensus on recommendations for the total elimination of nuclear weapons remains a matter of grave concern, the Commission's determination in sustaining structured dialogue and the willingness of states to remain engaged is crucial. We share the view that the total elimination of nuclear weapons is the only assurance against their proliferation, use, or threat of use. In so doing, we reaffirm our commitment to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, the Humanitarian Pledge for the Prohibition and Elimination of Nuclear Weapons, among many. We recognize the essential role of the International Atomic Energy Agency, which seeks to promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy and to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons through verification and safeguards. ensuring that such use do not serve military purposes. Since 1962, Liberia has remained a proud member of the IAEA, and we therefore encourage member states to deepen cooperation and promote the work of the agency. As a post-war country, Liberia is inclined to speak to the devastating effects of the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons. Their proliferation and illegal sales continue to destabilize many regions of the world, especially in Africa. I thank the distinguished representative of Iran for his statement. I now give the floor to her excellency, the permanent representative of Montenegro. Excellency, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Mr. Chair, Montenegro aligns itself with the EU statement and would like to highlight several points of particular importance to us. Maintaining international peace and security remains primary purpose of the UN. Yet today we are facing numerous conflicts around the world marked by violations and abuses of international law, including the international humanitarian and human rights law. These challenges are complex and must be resolved with our collective action. That is why Montenegro will continue to uphold the international law, the rule of law, and multilateralism based on the UN charter, while continuing to promote global security architecture for arms control, disarmament, and non-proliferation. We strongly believe that the implementation of the Pact for the Future provides an excellent platform to tackle current and future global challenges. The UNAD process can offer additional support to these efforts as it aims towards a more effective UN. Mr. Chair, we are heading towards the fourth year of Russia's unprovoked, illegal, and unjustified aggression against Ukraine. Once again, we strongly condemn Russia's violation of fundamental principles of international law that has negative global consequences and has caused immense destruction and loss of life. We are deeply concerned about the continued military support that Belarus, Iran and the DPRK provide to Russia, which enables sustainment of its illegal war of aggression. We reaffirm our call to Russia to respect international law and its international obligations, including those in disarmament and non-proliferation. At the same time, two years after the horrific October 7 terrorist attack, we welcome the ceasefire agreement in Gaza, which ensured the release of hostages and enables the delivery of humanitarian aid to those who need it most. We believe this is the first most important step to end the suffering and ensure durable peace in the Middle East. We are also deeply concerned by the deteriorating situation in other parts of the world that are overshadowed by the presence of war. Mr. Chair, Montenegro reaffirms its resolute commitment to arms control, disarmament, and non-proliferation, and the full implementation of the NPT under effective international control, goals that are enshrined in the UN Charter and at the heart of the multilateral security. As a state party to the NPT, CWC, BWC, ATT, and the UNCCW, Montenegro consistently advocates for universal adherence, effective implementation, and strengthening of these instruments. We view them not only as legal obligation, but as a moral and political imperative that should define our collective security architecture. Montenegro is actively strengthening its national CBRN resilience framework guided by our national CBRN Roadmap 2023-28. We are enhancing legislative alignment, national capacities and interagency coordination for preparedness and response in close cooperation with the EU's CBRN Centres of Excellence initiative. Most recently, Montenegro also formally notified the Australia Group of our decision to become unilaterally adherent to the AG guidelines on preventing biological and chemical weapons. We will continue to support the objectives and implementation of the CWC and the vital work of the OPCW in ensuring the complete elimination of chemical weapons and preventing their re-emergence. Additionally, we reaffirm our full commitment to the BWC and welcome continued dialogue on establishing a robust and effective verification mechanism to ensure compliance. Excellencies, Montenegro continues to support the full and effective implementation of the Convention on the Prohibition of the Use, Stockpiling, Production and Transfer of Anti-Personnel Mines and their Destruction. We welcome the progress achieved under the Convention, including the adoption of the new Action Plan 2025-29. We underline the importance of assistance for mine clearance, victim rehabilitation and mine risk education, efforts to which Montenegro continues to contribute to, both nationally and through regional cooperation in the Western Balkans. We reiterate firm support for the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons and its protocols, which seek to balance legitimate defence needs with the imperative to prevent human suffering. We also commend the ongoing work of the Group of Governmental Experts on Emerging Technologies in the Area of Law. Dear colleagues, Montenegro is actively pursuing a comprehensive and strategic approach to small arms and light weapons control and reduction in line with the UN program and regional commitments in the Western Balkans, most notably under the UNDP CSAC regional roadmap 2030. Our national efforts include enhanced stockpile management, export controls, and domestic legislation in order to prevent illicit proliferation, as well as voluntary destruction programs for surplus weapons. Montenegro also cooperates closely with our neighbors and international partners to improve information sharing, border control, and community awareness aimed at preventing diversion and misuse of small arms and light weapons. Next year, we will mark the 30th anniversary of the signing of a legally binding sub-regional arms control document, the Florence Agreement. Its successful implementation, with more than 10,000 pieces of heavy weapons destroyed and more than 830 inspections carried out, shows that we can build trust even in the current complex condition and deteriorated security situation in Europe. Mr. Chair, recognizing the importance of responsible views of cyberspace to global security, Montenegro fully support all UN and international efforts in that vein. We have adopted cybersecurity strategy and are improving national capacities by establishing cybersecurity agency. Montenegro is also a host of the regional Western Balkans Cyber Capacity Center in cooperation with France and Slovenia. We also support preventing all forms of violence against women and ensuring that all peace processes integrate gender perspectives and enable equal and meaningful participation of women. The WPS agenda must also evolve to address emerging challenges which disproportionately affect women and girls. In conclusion, we strongly believe that international peace and security depend on sustained progress in disarmament, non-proliferation, and arms control. Montenegro remains committed to cooperation with our allies and partners in advancing a vision of a safer and more secure world. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Montenegro for her statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of San Marino. You have the floor.

Mr. Chair, it's a real pleasure to congratulate you and all the members of the Bureau on your election. You can count on this delegation's full cooperation. San Marino aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union. Now I'd like to add some comments in my national capacity. Mr. Chair, San Marino is deeply worried about all the ongoing conflicts around the world, which continue to spread death, destruction, and immense suffering to civilians, trapping them in cycles of violence and trauma. Sadly, we have witnessed an alarming rise in civilian casualties in conflicts. The number of women and children killed has reached disgraceful figures. Civilians have been deliberately attacked. Starvation and rape have been used as weapons of war by parties. We firmly condemn such action and call on all parties to strictly abide to international humanitarian law. Regrettably, violence has increased also against humanitarian actors and journalists who are being killed in unprecedented numbers. We condemn the attacks against humanitarian personnel, aid workers and journalists. and we call on all parties to reverse the erosion of international humanitarian law. In this spirit, San Marino has recently endorsed the declaration for the protection of humanitarian personnel. San Marino also condemns the use of explosive weapons in populated areas, which causes the disruption of basic services for the population and unacceptable civilian harm. We continue to support and call for the implementation of the political declaration on strengthening the protection of civilians from the humanitarian consequences arising from the use of explosive weapons in populated areas. We also recall the fundamental importance of the Convention on Cluster Munitions and of the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention in preventing harm to civilians. We regret recent withdrawals from such instruments. We believe that in times of armed conflict, civilians are particularly at risk, and it is therefore critical to reinforce IHL. San Marino remains very concerned about the ongoing Russian aggression against Ukraine, which continues to cause dramatic consequences for the civilian population. We welcome all international efforts for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace, in line with the UN Charter and international law, and we continue to support Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders. Concerning the Middle East, Samarin is thankful to the successful mediator's efforts and welcomes the conclusion of the peace agreement. While remaining very concerned about the dire humanitarian situation in Gaza, this recent long-awaited outcome represents a glimmer of hope for a just and lasting peace based on the two-state solution. Mr. Chair, ongoing armed conflicts increase global instability and put all humanity at imminent risks, including nuclear risks. Aggressive nuclear rhetoric and threats have regrettably reappeared, increasing the risk of deadly escalation, threatening to spiral out of control and putting all humanity in global danger. San Marino condemns in the strongest terms any nuclear threat, implicit or explicit, and irrespective of circumstances. The catastrophic humanitarian consequences of any nuclear detonation must always guide our work. Regrettably, nuclear doctrines have been strengthened, and military and nuclear confrontation is growing. Modernization and expansion of nuclear arsenals are advancing, as it is clearly shown by the rising military expenditures. The use of new technologies, including artificial intelligence, creates new uncertainties and concerns, while the risks of cyber attacks and manipulation of nuclear arsenals cannot be underestimated. The Doomsday Clock warns 89 seconds to midnight, the closest it has ever been to global disaster. We need to change course. The only way to change this course is a collective recommitment to our multilateral instruments. San Marino continues being firmly committed to the full implementation of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, the cornerstone of nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation, and looks forward to the upcoming NPT Review Conference. We must seize this opportunity to uphold the integrity and credibility of this instrument and finally prove that when we work together constructively, we are able to achieve a successful outcome. San Marino firmly believes in a world free of nuclear weapons and firmly supports the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. This treaty, which complements and strengthens the disarmament regime, is an important step in our path towards a nuclear-free world. San Marino promptly signed and ratified this treaty, showing an unwavering support for a total ban of nuclear weapons. We urge all countries to join this important instrument. Mr. Chair, San Marino is also worried about the risks related to new technologies in the military domain. The rapid advances in artificial intelligence have led to concerning levels of autonomy in conflicts. We must ensure that human control is preserved over life and death decisions. The increasing use of autonomous weapon systems, which challenge human control over the use of force, has deepened humanitarian, legal, ethical, technological, security, and human rights concerns. San Marino believes that international regulations of autonomous weapons systems are urgently needed due to their rapid advancement and to their increasing use on the battlefield. We therefore support the starting of negotiations for a legally binding instrument, which should be based on the two-tier approach to set clear prohibitions and restrictions. Mr. Chair, We are witnessing an unprecedented rise in global military expenditures. San Marino believes that security cannot be based on an arms race. On the contrary, we believe that investing in disarmament, arms control, and non-proliferation in the long term will result in an investment in peace, security, and sustainable development. We must redirect our efforts towards that path. renewing our commitments to disarmament obligations and to peace through diplomacy and cooperation. Thank you for your attention.

I call on the representative of the Russian Federation.

We remind you that it is the fault of Western countries that there is a severe crisis raging in Europe that still has not been quelled. a crisis in which nuclear weapons states are involved. The hostile expanse of Western states and the creation of an anti-Russian bridgehead in Ukraine have jeopardized Russia's national security interests. The most fanatical European countries, including nuclear states, continue to spout inflammatory rhetoric, brandish their nuclear arsenals, seek means to damage Russia by proxy, hatch plans for provocation, and refuse to abandon the harmful expansion of NATO toward Russian borders, which for us poses a critical strategic risk. And thus, the risk of armed conflict between nuclear states is rising, which all the countries of the nuclear five pledged to prevent in accordance with the joint statement of January 3rd, 2022. What is this, if not irresponsible behavior that heightens the risk of armed conflict involving nuclear states, nuclear powers? One gets the impression that European states continue to believe in their unlimited capacity to control escalation and to exert military pressure on Russia without harm to themselves. This is an extremely dangerous delusion which could lead to catastrophic consequences. This is the essence of our signals and our warnings. I call on the representative of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, for giving me the floor. My delegation is taking the floor in response to the statements made by delegations of Italy and Greece, who blatantly slandered the DPRK's sovereign rights and defensive measures. DPRK has enshrined the possession of its nuclear weapons in its national law. And those member states should have to understand that they are committing acts of openly disregarding and grossly violating the sovereignty of the DPRK by calling for denuclearization of the DPRK. The concept of denuclearization of the DPRK has already lost its meaning and has gone forever. No matter how long and how ardently they are calling for denuclearization of DPRK, We will remain as a nuclear weapons state permanently. DPRK's nuclear deterrent has proved its capability for and reliability in defending the national sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the lives and the.

Safety of the peoples from foreign military.

Threats, aggression, and attack, steadily increase the security quite efficient on the Korean peninsula and in the region. Unless the nuclear threat to us coming from outside is terminated, and as long as there exist the imperialist forces that use the nukes for the means of existence of their tyranny, We will never allow an interruption on our road of bolstering our military capabilities to safeguard the security of our state and the well-being of our people, both at present and in the future, but continue to move forward to maintain the edge of our overwhelming strength. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I now call on the representative of Israel.

Thank you so much, Chair. We were not intending to take the floor again today, but my delegation is compelled to do so in relation to the statement by the Iranian representative. It is clear that the Iranian regime insists in speaking about Gaza to move away the focus from its own failures, from its extremist ideology, its brutality against the Iranian population, and its malign regional ambitions. It is not surprising therefore that last Monday, the Iranian representative was the only representative trying to defend Hamas atrocities. especially in a day that was marked by hope and opportunity and as Hamas was executing Gazan people in the streets. Syria, which has repeatedly expressed its desire to build partnerships on a basis of joint interests and within the framework of respect for international law and the purposes and objectives of the UN Charter and the implementation of United Nations resolutions. Syria needs in its path to recovery, it needs the support of the international community and not interference in its internal affairs. I thank you, Chair.

Iran's nuclear escalation has been detailed in more than 60 reports by the IAEA over six years.

It includes the accumulation of.

A high enriched uranium stockpile, which lacks any credible civilian justification and is unprecedented for a state without a nuclear weapons program. Thank you, Mr. Chair.

And add that the UN provisions reimposed on September 27th are not arbitrary, but instead narrowly scoped to address the threat posed by Iran's nuclear, missile, and conventional arms programs and support for terrorism. Their return does not preclude later removal through diplomacy. The United States remains open to direct talks with Iran to achieve a lasting, peaceful resolution to the nuclear issue. Iran must also fully comply and cooperate with the IAEA and fully implement its safeguards obligations. Thank you, Chair.
